title: Correlations in Data Drive Feature Geometry
one_liner: When an autoencoder compresses text patterns, repeated co-activations arrange features into semantic clusters and circles without needing explicit design.
lead: Inside language models, features (the model's learned concepts) are arranged in organized patterns—semantic clusters, ordered circles for months. Where do these patterns come from? This paper shows they emerge naturally when an autoencoder compresses sparse patterns from real text, purely to fit information through a narrow bottleneck.

problem.h2: Toy models don't match real models
paras: Early theories (using toy models—tiny, artificial setups) predicted that features would arrange themselves into regular geometric shapes like small dice or crystals. But real language models show something different: semantic clusters (words with related meanings grouped together) and ordered patterns (months arranged in sequence).

Researchers asked: where do these organized patterns come from? Current theories could not explain them. The naive guess was that the model must be learning these patterns because they help solve downstream tasks (for instance, keeping related animal words near each other might help the model answer questions about animals faster). But nobody had shown how compression alone, without any downstream task pressure, could create such organized arrangements.

callout.html: Can compression alone create the organized feature patterns we see in real language models?

steps.text: Extract which words appear together frequently (co-occurrence statistics from real text).
Train a neural network with a narrow layer (bottleneck) that forces compression.
Features that often activate together get pulled to nearby locations by the bottleneck pressure.
The hidden layer creates vectors (lists of numbers) for each feature; plot them and observe clusters and circles.
Compare to features extracted from actual language models; the patterns match without extra design.

paras: The paper rearranges feature representation (the list of numbers each feature gets) by tuning how tightly the autoencoder squeezes information through the bottleneck and whether training uses weight decay (a light penalty on large numbers). These changes cause features that co-activate in the data to end up in similar geometric regions.

hidden.h2: The co-firing structure (features that activate together)
hidden.name: Co-activation correlation (which features fire together)
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity: co-activation correlation—which features tend to activate (become non-zero) at the same time in the data. Words like dog and cat co-activate often; dog and arithmetic rarely do.

The paper estimates this from the text directly: count how often each pair of words appears together. This co-activation structure in the data is then mirrored in where features end up—features with high co-activation end up physically near each other in the learned representation.

heat.caption: Darker features co-activate more often; they sit near each other in space.

reads.html: Some words appear together constantly (dog in pet sentence); others never do (dog in calculus problem). The autoencoder learns this and groups features accordingly.
Linear superposition—features linearly encode the low-rank structure of word co-occurrence, arranging by co-activation patterns under compression.

paras: The autoencoder has three layers: input (sparse word vectors), bottleneck (narrow compressed layer), and output (reconstruction). The bottleneck acts like a narrow door: only the most important patterns fit through. When two features co-activate, squeezing them through the same narrow space physically pushes their compressed codes to overlap or sit near each other. Over training, the network exploits this: it puts co-activating features in adjacent positions to save space, because similar locations require similar stored information.

The mechanism is purely spatial: imagine packing suitcases into a tiny closet. Items you use together get stacked near each other because it saves space. No one told the network to cluster dog and cat; the bottleneck did it automatically by choosing the most efficient spatial arrangement.

stages.s: Features with high co-activation settle near each other
Organized patterns: clusters, circles, semantic structure

symbols: the sparse word vector (which words appear in this text)
what the autoencoder outputs (its guess at the original)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine a bottleneck of width 3 and two co-activating features (dog and cat).
Without penalty: network encodes dog at [0.8, 0.6, 0.1] and cat at [0.75, 0.65, 0.05], a bit overlapped.
With weight penalty (lambda=0.1): large numbers are discouraged, so the network pushes both closer together: dog=[0.5, 0.4, 0.0], cat=[0.5, 0.4, 0.0]. Identical positions save space.
High co-activation and bottleneck pressure force features to share geometric neighborhoods, creating clusters.

math.note: The weight penalty (regularization) acts like gravity pulling the numbers toward zero, so the network uses space more efficiently by bunching similar features together.

bars.h2: Comparison: toy models vs. this framework

charts.title: Old toy-model prediction
charts.note: Toy models predicted rigid, structured arrangements but missed semantic meaning.

charts.title: This paper (BOWS framework)
charts.note: Compression alone creates the organized patterns seen in real language models.

items.html: If the compressed layer is too large, features have plenty of space and no pressure to cluster. Arrangements remain scattered and random.
Without the penalty on large numbers, the network wastes space on redundant features and doesn't force efficient packing. Clusters blur and disappear.
If the training data has different word patterns than the language model being studied (e.g., training on finance text when studying a general model), the patterns won't match.
With pressure to compress and a dataset matching the model's training patterns, features arrange into semantic clusters and coherent spatial patterns.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train a small sparse autoencoder on co-occurrence statistics extracted from a text corpus (e.g., the 1000 most common words from Wikipedia). Use a narrow bottleneck (e.g., 20-dimensional compressed space for 1000 words) and include a weight penalty. After training, extract the learned feature vectors and visualize them in 2D (using a technique like t-SNE). The demo must show semantic clustering (animal words cluster together, food words cluster nearby, etc.) and if training long enough, ordered patterns (numbers 1–10 arranged in a line).
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss: compression alone, without any explicit instruction, produces the organized patterns observed in real language model internals.
